pending_articles.title: Probing the neural geometry of conscious object perception in time
pending_articles.content: Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a "coarse-to-fine" sequence or a "fine-to-coarse" sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. By contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level.
pending_articles.author: Hachisuka, A., Baumgarten, T. J., Spector, D., Koenig, L., He, B. J.

pending_articles.title: Distinct genetic requirements underlie LITE-1-dependent photosensation and avoidance of high concentration of diacetyl in C. elegans
pending_articles.content: The eyeless nematode C. elegans can detect and respond to aversive blue and ultraviolet light using the gustatory receptor homolog LITE-1. In addition to its role in phototransduction, LITE-1 also functions as a chemoreceptor for the odorants diacetyl and 2,3-pentanedione. However, whether these different sensory modalities rely on the same downstream signalling components is unknown. In this study, we provide behavioural evidence that unlike its LITE-1-dependent photosensory function which relies on cGMP signalling components, its chemosensory function remains intact in mutants with disrupted cGMP signalling.

pending_articles.title: Endothelial CD36 links arteriolar remodeling to metabolic and immune alterations in Alzheimer's disease
pending_articles.content: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is accompanied by profound cerebrovascular dysfunction, yet it remains unclear whether endothelial abnormalities reflect only vascular injury or altered regulatory states connecting vascular remodeling with metabolic and immune function. We integrated human brain transcriptomic and histopathological data with complementary mouse genetic and human iPSC-derived endothelial models to examine a CD36-centered endothelial-state framework in AD. Analysis of the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas identified three CD36-expressing endothelial populations; intermediate-CD36 Endo 2 predominated in both reference and AD samples, although the relative subset distributions differed. In hippocampal and cortical tissue from six AD patients, endothelial CD36 expression was observed in structurally abnormal arterioles with disrupted mural organization. In complementary mouse studies, endothelial PKD1 deficiency was accompanied by increased vascular CD36 and cerebrovascular abnormalities, whereas endothelial CD36 deletion altered lipid-metabolic and innate-immune-associated transcriptional programs, including AD-relevant genes and pathways, under metabolic-inflammatory stress. To assess whether distinct human endothelial backgrounds remained pharmacologically responsive, we treated control and CRISPR-engineered PSEN1 E276A iPSC-derived ECs with GS4898, a small molecule previously linked to arterial specification. Both maintained endothelial identity but displayed different baseline transcriptional profiles and shared as well as cell-line-dependent responses to GS4898. Together, our study identifies a CD36-associated vascular phenotype in human AD, demonstrates CD36-dependent regulation of brain endothelial metabolic-immune transcriptional programs in vivo, and reveals endothelial transcriptional responsiveness to pharmacologic perturbation. The observed endothelial transcriptional plasticity may provide a basis for developing state-selective therapeutic strategies targeting cerebrovascular dysfunction in AD.

pending_articles.title: Cross-state stability and maturational similarity of the social brain connectome in children and adolescents
pending_articles.content: The intra-individual stability of functional connectivity (FC) across two or more scans and the inter-individual similarity of FC patterns relative to peers capture developmental variability in functional brain organization. Despite their different referents, these measures are strongly coupled at the whole brain level; however, it remains unclear whether this relationship emerges in development, whether it extends to the social brain, and whether it differs by sex. Based on the importance of social development in this age range, we hypothesized that known developmental relationships and sex-specific effects would be more pronounced in the social brain relative to the whole brain. Using a large psychiatrically enriched sample of 769 youth ages 6-21 (female N = 327, mean age = 12.27 years), we computed FC during rest and movie-watching scans and quantified stability across scans as well as similarity to mature subjects (n=36) within each condition. We then tested whether sex-dependent age relationships were captured by these measures or by the strength of their coupling. Our results showed that cross-state stability and maturational similarity are strongly coupled in development, and that this coupling is enhanced in the social brain relative to the whole brain. Furthermore, the strength of stability-similarity coupling increased as a function of age in females, while males showed the opposite effect. When assessing relationships between age and each FC measure independently, no individual effects were significant after FDR correction. However, our multivariate age-prediction models fared much better, demonstrating that edgewise stability and maturational similarity measures can capture spatially heterogeneous developmental effects that are lost when collapsing across edges. Together, these results support the emerging idea that the degree of FC stability across scans is related to how closely an individuals functional architecture aligns to a shared template. Here, we newly show that this stability-similarity coupling is stronger in the social brain and varies with age in sex-specific ways. Future longitudinal work is needed to establish whether these cross-sectional relationships also characterize within-person developmental change.

Context-Dependent Functional Diversity of Dorsomedial Posterior Parietal Neurons Revealed by Single-Unit FMRI Mapping during Naturalistic Viewing
pending_articles.content: The dorsomedial posterior parietal cortex (dmPPC) plays an important role in episodic processing by integrating sensory, cognitive, and motor information across distributed brain systems. However, how individual dmPPC neurons participate in large-scale functional organization during naturalistic experience remains poorly understood. To address this question, we combined single-unit electrophysiology and awake fMRI in five rhesus macaques of both sexes viewing identical naturalistic video stimuli. Using single-unit fMRI mapping, we generated whole-brain neuron–BOLD functional maps by correlating individual neuronal activity with voxel-wise fMRI signals across the brain. We found that neuron–BOLD functional maps exhibited strong context-dependent organization, with neurons recorded during the same video context showing substantially greater similarity than neurons recorded during different video conditions. Compared with neuronal spiking activity or critical fMRI frames alone, neuron–BOLD functional maps more robustly captured contextual structure. Despite this shared large-scale organization, a substantial subset of neighboring neurons recorded simultaneously from the same electrode displayed markedly distinct whole-brain association patterns, revealing substantial local functional heterogeneity within the dmPPC. This local heterogeneity was not readily explained by waveform-based putative cell class or by opposing neuronal firing dynamics. In addition, distributed cortical and medial temporal regions exhibited highly context-dependent neuron–BOLD association patterns during naturalistic viewing. Together, these findings demonstrate that dmPPC neurons participate in dynamic and heterogeneous large-scale functional organization during naturalistic episodic processing. More broadly, this study establishes single-unit fMRI mapping as a framework for linking single-neuron activity to distributed whole-brain dynamics across contextual conditions.

pending_articles.title: Midbrain Glutamatergic Neurons Modulate the Acoustic Startle Reflex and Prepulse Inhibition in Mice
pending_articles.content: Prepulse inhibition (PPI) of the acoustic startle reflex is a widely used operational measure of sensorimotor gating that is disrupted in several neuropsychiatric disorders. PPI deficits are a hallmark feature of schizophrenia, often associated with attentional and cognitive impairments. Although PPI is extensively used in translational and preclinical research, the cellular and circuit mechanisms underlying this phenomenon remain incompletely understood, even under physiological conditions. Recent evidence suggests that noncholinergic projections from the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPTg) to the caudal pontine reticular nucleus (PnC) contribute to PPI. Here, we investigated the role of PPTg glutamatergic neurons in acoustic startle and PPI. Tract tracing, immunohistochemical analyses, and in vitro whole-cell recordings in wild-type male and female mice demonstrated that PPTg glutamatergic neurons innervate the PnC and establish excitatory synapses onto PnC neurons. Optogenetic inhibition of PPTg->PnC glutamatergic synapses in vivo increased PPI across interstimulus intervals (ISIs) without altering baseline startle responses. In contrast, optogenetic activation of this pathway did not modify PPI. However, activation of PPTg–PnC glutamatergic projections instead of an acoustic prepulse bidirectionally modulated startle responses in a time-dependent manner, suppressing startle at short ISIs while enhancing startle at longer intervals. Additionally, while PPTg glutamatergic inputs target PnC glycinergic neurons, our in vitro whole-cell recordings combined with optogenetic stimulation at PPTg->PnC synapses revealed that PPTg glutamatergic inputs also activate PnC glutamatergic giant neurons. Together, our findings identify a novel temporally dependent excitatory mechanism within the brainstem startle circuit, through which PPTg glutamatergic neurons modulate sensorimotor gating.

pending_articles.title: Dynamic Reduction of Neural Uncertainty Shapes Perceptual Decisions in a Bayes-Optimal Manner
pending_articles.content: Fast and accurate decisions are fundamental for adaptive behavior. Theories of decision-making posit that evidence in favor of different choices is gradually accumulated until a critical value is reached. It remains unclear, however, which aspects of the neural code get updated during evidence accumulation. Here we investigated whether evidence accumulation relies on a gradual increase in the precision of neural representations of sensory input (i.e., a decrease in neural uncertainty). Healthy human volunteers (N = 32, 24 females) discriminated global motion direction over a patch of moving dots, and their brain activity was recorded using electroencephalography. Time-resolved neural uncertainty was estimated using multivariate feature-specific analyses of brain activity. Behavioral measures were modeled using iterative Bayesian inference (BI) either on its own (i.e., the full model) or by swapping free model parameters with neural uncertainty estimates derived from brain recordings. The neurally restricted model was further refitted using randomly shuffled neural uncertainty. The full model and the unshuffled neural model yielded very good and comparable fits to the data, whereas the shuffled neural model yielded worse fits. Taken together, the findings reveal that the brain relies on reducing neural uncertainty during decision-making. They also provide neurobiological support for BI as a fundamental computational mechanism in support of decision-making.

recently_processed.title: Temporal RNA splicing dysregulation in a human multicellular model of C9orf72 ALS
recently_processed.content: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a complex and heterogenous disease, comprising of familial and sporadic forms, numerous genetic mutations, and a wide range of affected cell types and proposed dysregulated processes. While the usage of in vitro cell cultures, mouse models, and postmortem patient tissue have advanced our understanding of ALS disease mechanisms, the temporal progression of the disease and how early molecular changes evolve remain poorly understood. Here, we establish human spinal cord organoids (hSpO) derived from C9orf72 patient induced pluripotent stem cells (C9-ALS hiPSCs) as a platform to model longitudinal changes across the disease trajectory. We show that C9-ALS hSpO recapitulate hallmark C9orf72-related pathologies, increased cell death, and progressive neuronal dysfunction. We further identify RNA splicing dysregulation as an early and persistent feature of C9-ALS, with splicing signatures in hSpO closely mirroring those observed in postmortem patient tissue. Finally, prediction of RNA binding proteins (RBPs) that induce early splicing changes in C9-ALS reveals signatures consistent with a broad RBP network dysfunction. Together, this work establishes hSpO as an in vitro system for investigating early disease mechanisms of ALS in a human multicellular context and highlights dysregulated events that precede cell death.

recently_processed.title: New software package: ERPLAB Studio
recently_processed.content:
We are excited to announce the release of a new EEG/ERP analysis package, ERPLAB Studio. We think it’s a huge improvement over the classic EEGLAB user interface. See our cheesy “advertisement” video to get a quick overview.

Rather than operating as an EEGLAB plugin, ERPLAB Studio is a standalone Matlab program that provides a more efficient and user-friendly interface to the most commonly used EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines.

With ERPLAB Studio, you automatically see the EEG or ERP waveforms as soon as you load a file. And as soon as you perform an operation, you see what the new EEG/ERP looks like. For example, when you filter the data, you immediately see the filtered waveforms.

You can even select multiple datasets and apply an operation like artifact detection on all of them in one step. And then you can immediately see the results, such as which EEG epochs have been marked with artifacts.

We give you access to EEGLAB’s ICA-based artifact correction tools, but with a nice bonus. You can plot the ICA activations in the same window with the EEG data, making it easy to see which ICA components correspond to specific artifacts such as eyeblinks.

The program has an EEG tab for processing continuous and epoched EEG data, and an ERP tab for processing averaged ERPs.

The automatic ERP plotting makes it easy for you to view the data laid out according to the electrode locations. And we have an Advanced Waveform Viewer that can make publication-quality plots.

ERPLAB Studio is mainly just a new user interface. Under the hood, we’re running the same EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines you’ve always used. And scripting is identical.

ERPLAB Studio is included in version 11 and higher of ERPLAB. You simply follow our download/installation instructions and then type estudio from the Matlab command line.

If you’re new to ERPLAB, we strongly recommend that you go through our tutorial before starting to process your own data.

If you already know how to use the original version of ERPLAB (which we now call ERPLAB Classic), you can quickly learn how to use ERPLAB Studio with our Transition Guide.

We also have a manual that describes every feature in detail.

recently_processed.title: Assistive Trajectory Planning for Lower Limb Exoskeletons: Strategies From Laboratory-Optimized Gait to Environmentally-Adaptive Locomotion Through Multimodal Parameter Awareness
recently_processed.content: Lower limb assistive exoskeletons (LLEs) show great potential to reduce metabolic cost, improve walking performance, and correct abnormal gait patterns. Among their core control architectures, assistive trajectory planning is key to determining system responsiveness and effectiveness under varying locomotion conditions. Many trajectory planning methods were proposed in either laboratory or unstructured real-world environments. To clarify the scope and challenges of existing research, this review categorizes trajectory planning strategies into two major types based on application scenarios: (1) strategies for laboratory settings with controllable disturbances, which usually involve optimal control for gait under stable or controllable conditions; and (2) strategies for real-world environments characterized by varying terrain, individual differences, and gait fluctuations, which usually involve adaptive control for gait under diverse or unstructured conditions. Given the foundational role of gait phase detection in trajectory planning, this review also systematically examines mainstream algorithms for gait phase recognition and estimation. Finally, the paper analyzes the limitations of existing methods and discusses the potential of advanced algorithms, intelligent multimodal sensing systems, novel sensing technologies, and embedded deployment to enhance the performance of exoskeleton assistive trajectory planning.
